title: The body, aches, and little words
goal: Describing your symptoms to a doctor, naming parts of the body — and putting in place four little words that sit mid-sentence in place of full pronouns.
bekal: name parts of the body and say where it hurts
use the clitic pronouns مې، دې، یې، مو
get by at the pharmacy and the clinic

dialogs.title: خبرې اترې — په روغتون کې
dialogs.intro: Budi wakes up with a throat that refuses to cooperate. Zarghuna takes him to a small clinic two lanes from home.

lines.speaker: ډاکټر:
lines.id: Welcome. What seems to be the problem?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ستونی مې خوږېږي او سر مې دروند دی.
lines.baca: stūnay me khwaẓīẓī aw sar me drūnd day.
lines.id: My throat hurts and my head feels heavy.
lines.literal: throat of-mine hurts and head of-mine heavy is.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: له دوو ورځو راهیسې. پرون تبه هم راغله.
lines.baca: lə dwo wradzo rāhīse. parūn taba ham rāghla.
lines.id: For two days. Yesterday a fever came too.
lines.literal: from two days-from since. yesterday fever also came-FEM.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: آه... درد یې ډېر دی کله چې تېروم.
lines.baca: āh... dard ye ḍer day kəla che terawəm.
lines.id: Aah... it really hurts when I swallow.
lines.literal: ah... pain of-it much is when that swallow-I.

lines.speaker: ډاکټر:
lines.text: ستونی مو سور دی. سختې پرېشانۍ خبره نه ده.
lines.baca: stūnay mo sūr day. sakhte pareṣānəy khabara nə da.
lines.id: Your throat is red. Nothing to worry about.
lines.literal: throat of-yours red is. serious worry thing not is.

lines.speaker: ډاکټر:
lines.text: هو. دا دوا ورځ کې درې ځله واخلئ، درې ورځې.
lines.baca: ho. dā dawā wradz ke dre dzala wākhləy, dre wradze.
lines.id: Yes. Take this medicine three times a day, for three days.
lines.literal: yes. this medicine day in three times take-you, three days.

lines.speaker: ډاکټر:
lines.text: وروسته. او ګرمې اوبه ډېرې وڅښئ.
lines.baca: wrūsta. aw garme ūba ḍere wə́tsṣəy.
lines.id: After. And drink lots of warm water.
lines.literal: after. and warm water much drink-you.

lines.speaker: زرغونه:
lines.text: شین چای د شاتو سره ورکړم؟
lines.baca: shīn chāy də shāto sara warkṛəm?
lines.id: Shall I give him green tea with honey?
lines.literal: green tea of honey with give-I?

lines.speaker: ډاکټر:
lines.text: ډېره ښه. دا زمونږ تر ټولو زوړ درمل دی.
lines.baca: ḍera ṣa. dā zmūẓ tər ṭolo zoṛ darmal day.
lines.id: Very good. That's our oldest medicine.
lines.literal: very good. this of-ours from all old medicine is.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: مننه، ډاکټر صاحب. فیس څومره دی؟
lines.baca: manana, ḍākṭar sāhib. fīs tsomra day?
lines.id: Thank you, Doctor. How much is it?
lines.literal: thank-you, doctor sir. cost how-much is?

lines.speaker: ډاکټر:
lines.text: دوه سوه افغانۍ. خدای دې روغ لره.
lines.baca: dwa swa afghānəy. khudāy de rogh lara.
lines.id: Two hundred afghani. May God keep you healthy.
lines.literal: two hundred afghani. God may healthy keep.

notes: Look at the little word **مې** in the second line. ستونی **مې** خوږېږي means "my throat hurts", and مې replaces زما. It's shorter, far more common in speech, and never stands at the start of a sentence.

⚠️ Clitic pronouns always stand **in second place**, right after the first word of the sentence — just like به in unit 14. If the sentence opens with a noun, the clitic sticks right after that noun: سر **مې** دروند دی.

Pashto doesn't say "I have a headache". It says سر مې خوږېږي, literally "my head hurts" — the body part is the subject, not the person. This is the same pattern as خوښېږي in unit 15, and the same as in Persian and Urdu.
The word تبه (fever) is feminine, so the sentence is تبه هم **راغله**, with the feminine form. Pashto says a fever "comes", not that you "have" one — and the phrase sounds livelier than the English.
The phrase له کله راهیسې means "since when". راهیسې always pairs with له in front of it, one more pair that works like those in unit 6. The answer uses the oblique form: له دوو ورځو راهیسې.
The blessing خدای دې روغ لره means "may God keep you healthy", and it's said both to sick people and as a warm thank-you. Just answer مننه.

grammars.title: Four clitic pronouns
body: Clitic pronouns replace full pronouns for possession, for objects, and for the doer of a past sentence with an object. These four words are among the most frequent in everyday Pashto, and recognizing them multiplies how much you can catch.
⚠️ The placement rule is absolute: **never at the start of a sentence**, always in second place. If the sentence opens with نه or به, the clitic stands right after that word.

grammars.title: Saying where it hurts
body: The pattern is fixed: body part, clitic, then the verb **خوږېږي** (hurts, aches). The body part is the subject, so the verb agrees with it — not with the person.
If more than one thing hurts, the verb is plural: سترګې مې **خوږېږي** (my eyes hurt, since سترګې is plural). This follows straight on from the pattern you set up in unit 15.

sections.title: Parts of the body, and at the clinic

blocks.title: Phrases you need if you fall ill abroad
items: Opening: **زه ناروغ یم** *zə nārogh yəm* — "I'm ill". A woman says زه ناروغه یم.
Explaining: **... مې خوږېږي** with the body part in front. If you forget the word, just point and say **دلته مې خوږېږي** — "it hurts here".
Asking how to take it: **ورځ کې څو ځله؟** *wradz ke tso dzala* — "how many times a day?" and **له ډوډۍ وړاندې که وروسته؟** — "before or after meals?".
Mentioning an allergy: **زه ... ته حساسیت لرم** *zə ... ta hassāsiyat larəm* — "I'm allergic to ...". This one is worth memorizing before you travel, not after.
⚠️ Afghan pharmacies sell many medicines without a prescription, but that's no license to guess. Describe your symptoms, ask for advice, and ask the name of the medicine.

blocks.title: Clitics in everyday conversation
items: For possession, the clitic almost always wins over the long form. Afghans say **نوم مې بودي دی**, and very rarely زما نوم بودي دی — the second is correct but sounds like reading aloud.
In past stories, the clitic replaces the oblique doer from unit 13: **ولیدل مې** means "I saw it", and it's the form you'll hear most.
The word **یې** does the most work: it can mean "his/her", "him/her" as an object, and "he/she" as a past doer. Context separates them, and your ear will learn faster than your head.
⚠️ Don't use a clitic when your sentence opens with the part you want to stress. If you want to insist "MINE, not his", use the long form زما — the long form is the emphatic form.

exercises.prompt: Fix the position of the clitic.
Name the body part in Pashto.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: سر مې خوږېږي. — ستونی مې خوږېږي. — نوم دې څه دی؟ — نوم یې احمد دی. — ګېډه مې خوږېږي.
سر مې خوږېږي. — نوم دې څه دی؟ — نوم یې احمد دی. — ستونی مو سور دی. — ګېډه مې خوږېږي.
سر مې خوږېږي. — زه ناروغ یم. — زه تبه لرم. — دوا پکار ده. — ستونی مو سور دی.
wave: Touch five parts of your own body and say their names out loud, then say ... مې خوږېږي for each one. A sentence you learn before you're ill is the one that will be there when you really need it.
